newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Belo distances himself from politics.
newsitem.headline: Belo distances himself from politics.

text.p: Nobel Peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo on Friday tried to distance himself from the controversy surrounding this year's prize, turning to spiritual issues and away from political ones.
At a news conference shortly before co-winner Jose Ramos Horta met the press, Belo said political questions should be addressed to Horta, with whom he shares the $1.1 million prize.

"You ask (political questions) to Ramos Horta. This is the political leader...My profound desire is that we live in peace for the fulfilment of our human rights. We hope there is peace, reconciliation and justice."
Ramos Horta, a self-exiled East Timor independence campaigner, has accused Jakarta of pressuring Belo not to use this week's awards ceremony in Oslo to attack Indonesia.

Indonesia, which invaded East Timor in December 1975 and annexed it seven months later, condemned the Norwegian Nobel Committee's decision to include the veteran resistance leader in the prestigious prize.
Belo urged the world to look at how the East Timorese have been treated since 1975.
"I implore all men of goodwill to check for themselves the reports of the deplorable ways the East Timorese have been treated during these 21 years," he read from a statement.

"I regard this Nobel peace prize of 1996 as a precious gift to all those people in East Timor who long for and want justice and peace in their hearts...The peace prize is also for all Indonesians who fight or struggle for openness, for democracy for a respect of human rights in Indonesia," he added.

"I must admit that when I received the news of being bestowed this honour, it was with mixed feelings. From now on maybe the international community no longer would regard me as first and foremost as the Bishop...but rather more as a political figure.
"I am not a political figure. I am a bishop, I am a man of the church," he said.

Ramos Horta said two assassination attempts on Belo's life -- that Belo acknowledged in an earlier interview had occurred in 1989 and 1991 -- were evidence that Belo needed protection from the international community.
"He has been subjected to several assassination attempts. The Indonesians tried to assassinate him -- twice at least," Ramos Horta told a news conference.

"I do not need much protection anyway. The problem is with Bishop Belo -- he's the one who has to go back to East Timor, he's the one who needs protection. He needs all international protection possible."
Belo said the Nobel prize had sent a signal to Jakarta and in the future it would be more open to international pressure.
"I think they got the message from these Nobel awards...in the future they will be open to hear the community pressure -- the international community."
Asked why the two winners had not held a joint news conference, Ramos Horta said that Indonesia was pressuring Belo not to make appearances with him.
Ramos Horta said he had called on governments for economic sanctions against Indonesia as well as sanctions at the consumer level against companies with manufacturing operations in Indonesia.

"We appeal to individual consumers to impose their own sanctions -- that is, individuals who go to the supermarket...should not purchase goods that are manufactured in Indonesia at the cost of slave labour."
